title: Love's example
hookLine: Abelard stressed the cross as love so great it changes us

lines: CERTAINLY THIS WAS A RIGHTEOUS MAN.
cards: A Roman officer is on duty at an execution. The Gospels don't say what he expected. But this death goes differently.

Luke says that from the cross Jesus prays for the people killing him: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." When it's over, the officer, a centurion, says something nobody ordered him to say.
Luke records it: "Certainly this was a righteous man." Nothing was paid to him. No argument convinced him.
He watched how someone loved, all the way to the end, and Luke says he glorified God.

teach.h: WHAT DOES THE CROSS DO TO US?
teach.b: Moral influence is the name later writers gave to a picture stressed by Peter Abelard, a teacher in medieval Paris. The last few days asked what the cross does to death, to a debt, to a penalty.
Abelard asked what it does to us. His answer, in a commentary on Paul's letter to the Romans: the cross is God's love shown so plainly that it wins our love in return, and that love sets us free.

He leaned on a verse from that letter: "But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." Commendeth means shows, puts on display. Not after we cleaned up.
While we were yet sinners. Love goes first, and in this picture, love answers.
Jesus said, in John's Gospel, "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends." Here the cross is that greater love, and seeing it changes the one who sees.
People argued with Abelard in his own day.

Bernard of Clairvaux worried this made the cross only an example, a beautiful one, but no rescue. Some readers of Abelard point out that he spoke of more than example: he called this love a real power that frees.
Churches can keep this note inside their other pictures: whatever else the cross does, it shows love. The centurion's line is this picture in one sentence: he watched, and he spoke.

how: Some Christians meditate on the cross as a sign of God's love, for example in Good Friday services, hymns about the cross, and the Stations of the Cross, letting what they see shape how they treat others.

the cross as a rule book for good behavior

games.q: you're the centurion. the man you've just crucified prayed for his killers. it's over. what do you do?
o: finish the shift and say nothing.
speak up: certainly this was a righteous man.
games.why: Luke says he glorified God and said, "certainly this was a righteous man." nobody ordered it. he watched, and he spoke.

practice: Bring to mind one person who reliably sets you off, and picture the moment it usually happens.

Before the usual reaction, picture being loved first, while you were still at your worst, and let one small different response come: a pause, a softer word, a question instead of a verdict. If you pray, you can ask for that love.

wordCard.voice: Moral influence. The picture of the cross as love shown so plainly that it wins our love and changes us, stressed by Abelard.

carryVoice: Your line: love that changes us. In this picture, love goes first, and love answers. Until tomorrow.
